query: For high-entropy nanoalloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve structural and chemical stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of refractory metals such as hafnium and molybdenum to high-entropy alloys can improve their structural and chemical stability at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a composition such as Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 (at.%)
generation.intervention: Addition of small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.%) of refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum
generation.mechanism: The refractory metals enhance the mechanical properties of the alloy by forming a beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure
generation.baseline: The base alloy Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 (at.%) without the addition of refractory metals
generation.boundary: The temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which the refractory metals improve the alloy's properties are not fully understood and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of refractory metals does not result in improved high-temperature strength and stability, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
